text: Two students finish the same project. One says: my model gets ninety percent!
The other says: mine went from eight percent, to fifteen.
Easy. Ninety wins. Right?
You might be surprised.
Hold that thought. Because now it’s your turn: your own task, your own model, with your name on it.
The capstone. Episode one.
So what do I actually have to do?
Five things. Pick a task with answers code can check. Measure how a small model does on it.
Train it with GRPO. Then measure again, on puzzles it never saw in training. Accuracy and length.
And share it on Hugging Face, with a short write-up a curious friend could follow.
The task is the biggest decision you’ll make. Think Goldilocks.
Too hard, and the model never gets one right. Every group scores zero, and nothing is learned.
Too easy, and it’s always right. Nothing to learn there either.
Aim for a base model that scores somewhere between about five and sixty percent.
And the answers have to be checkable, by a checker I can actually write.
Yes. Lots of puzzles you can generate, with short answers. And run fifty puzzles before anything else.
The starter repo comes with three tasks that pass every test.
Countdown, the numbers game. Unit conversions. And tiny logic puzzles.
Use one, make one harder, or invent your own.
But skip anything where correct is a matter of opinion. Summaries, jokes, essays.
Because there’s no honest checker for a joke.
Then you cross six stepping stones, M zero to M five.
A self-test. Your task, and a reward you’ve attacked. A baseline.
A fifty-step pilot run. The full run. And sharing.
Why so many little steps?
So you never spend two hours of GPU time on a run that was broken from the start.
Milestone one has a fun rule: before you trust your reward, try to fool it.
Write just the target. Use a number twice. Skip one. Slip in some code.
Zero, zero, zero, zero! It caught every one.
That’s what a good reward does.
And if it doesn’t, you’ve just saved yourself a run that learns to cheat.
Then you hand in two things: your model on Hugging Face, and a write-up of three to eight hundred words.
It’s graded in five areas, four points each. Twenty in total.
Fourteen is a pass. Eighteen is a distinction.
So, back to our two students.
Ninety percent, with no baseline and no samples. Or eight to fifteen, reported honestly.
Pause, and have a guess.
Still A. A higher number has to win. Doesn’t it?
Nope. It’s B. There is no minimum accuracy.
A ninety with nothing to compare it to tells us nothing. A small, honest gain, with a failure explained, tells us a lot.
So the rubric rewards the why, not the score.
Exactly. Plus three hard rules. Test puzzles never in training. Every number from a run you actually did. And name the base model.
Quick recap.
Pick a task code can check, in the Goldilocks zone.
Cross the stones one at a time, and attack your own reward first.
And honest beats impressive.
Want to see one done, start to finish? We did one, on Countdown.
And while making it, we tried one more answer on our own checker.
Sixty-six equals twenty plus seven plus twenty-one plus eighteen. And it says... wrong?!
A perfectly correct answer. Scored as wrong. By our own checker.
Wait. A bug in your checker? What does that do to the training?
